1.note: The author is using the phrase **And it happened** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

The author is using **the return of the year** as a common expression of his culture to refer to the beginning of a new year. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [at the time of the start of the next year]
It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [at the start of the next year]

The people in this culture considered that a new year began in the spring, when they could once again start the cycle of planting and harvesting crops. You could indicate this in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in the spring]

The author is using **going out** as a common expression of his culture to mean “going to war.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the season when kings go to war]

The author is using the possessive form to describe an **army** that was characterized by **might**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a mighty army]
See how you translated the similar expression in 18:11. Alternate translation: [the Ammonites]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:46. Alternate translation: [And Joab defeated Rabbah] or [And Joab conquered Rabbah]

2.note: A **kikkar** of gold weighed about 34 kilograms or 75 pounds. In your translation, you could use the ancient measurement and spell the word “kikkar” the way it sounds in your language. You could also use the metric measurement given in the UST or use the measurement that your language and culture customarily use. Alternatively, you could use the ancient measurement and put a modern measurement in parentheses in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and its weight was 34 kilograms of gold] or [and its weight was 75 pounds of gold]

It is possible that this expression describes the value of the crown rather than its weight, since a crown weighing 34 kilograms or 75 pounds would have been too heavy to wear. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and it was worth a kikkar of gold] or [and it was worth 34 kilograms of gold]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. He seems to be noting one particular **precious stone** of exceptional value that was in the crown. (One Jewish historian says that it was a very large sardonyx.) This does not mean that there were not other precious stones in the crown as well. Alternate translation: [and one of the stones it contained was especially precious]

3.note: The author is using the pronoun **one** in a general sense, not to refer to a specific person. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and they sawed with saws]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they worked with picks of iron and with saws]

The word translated as **saws** represents the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense, since the author has already mentioned the **saw** earlier in the verse. The parallel verse in 2 Samuel 12:31 reads “axes.” Since the difference involves only one letter, it is possible that the word was changed in the process of copying and that the text originally read “axes” here. The UST follows that interpretation. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [and with axes]
In this context, the term **people** means “soldiers.” Alternate translation: [the soldiers]

4.note: This expression represents the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. It is possible that the author is speaking of a **battle** as if it were a living thing that could have **stood up**. However, this expression does not occur anywhere else in the Hebrew Bible. The parallel verse in 2 Samuel 21:18 reads “there was battle again.” Since the letters are very similar, it is possible that the wording was changed in the process of copying. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [that there was battle again]
To translate the term **struck** here and in verses 5 and 7, see how you translated it in the similar context in 4:43. Alternate translation: [Then Sibbecai the Hushathite killed]

**Sippai** is a variant spelling of the name “Saph,” which occurs in the parallel passage in 2 Samuel 21:18. Recall whether your translation team decided to use the same name for a given person in each instance where it appears or whether you decided to use the name that the biblical author does, even if that is a variant. Alternate translation: [Saph]
The author is using the term **children** to mean the “descendants” of Rapha. Alternate translation: [who was a descendant of Rapha]

The author assumes that readers will understand because **Sippai** was a descendant of Rapha, he was a giant as his ancestor had been. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. The UST models one way to do that.
The pronoun **they** refers to the **Philistines**, not to the **Raphaites**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the Philistines were subdued]

The expression **were subdued** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and the Israelites subdued them] or [and the Israelites subdued the Philistines]

5.q: וַ⁠יַּ֞ךְ אֶלְחָנָ֣ן בֶּן־יעור אֶת־לַחְמִי֙ אֲחִי֙ גָּלְיָ֣ת הַ⁠גִּתִּ֔י וְ⁠עֵ֣ץ חֲנִית֔⁠וֹ כִּ⁠מְנ֖וֹר אֹרְגִֽים
5.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about the **spear** that **Lahmi** had before the information that **Elhanan** **struck** him. Alternate translation: [Lahmi, the brother of Goliath the Gittite, had a spear whose wood was like a beam of weavers. But Elhanan, the son of Jair, struck him]

A **beam of weavers** was the thick, strong beam on which weavers hung their fabric. If your readers would not be familiar with this, in your translation you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a general expression. If you have already translated the book of 1 Samuel, see how you translated the similar expression in 1 Samuel 17:7. Alternate translation: [was like the thick, strong beam on which weavers hang their fabric]

6.note: The author is using the possessive form to describe a **man** who was characterized by great **stature** or height. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a very tall man]

The author is repeating the information about the number of digits that this **man of stature had**, presenting it in two different forms to emphasize how striking it is. You may find it appropriate to repeat the information in your translation in order to convey that emphasis, even if this would otherwise be extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. Alternate translation: [were 6 and 6, for a total of 24 digits in all]

The author means that this man had **six** **digits** on each of his hands and on each of his feet. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and he had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot]

The expression **was born** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And he too was a descendant of Rapha]

7.note: **Shimeah**, not **Jonathan**, was **the brother of David**. Your may have a kinship term that you can use to make this clear in your translation. Alternate translation: [Jonathan son of Shimeah, the nephew of David]

**Shimea** is a variant spelling of the name “Shimei,” which occurs in the parallel passage in 2 Samuel 21:21. Recall whether your translation team decided to use the same name for a given person in each instance where it appears or whether you decided to use the name that the biblical author does, even if that is a variant. Alternate translation: [Shimei]

8.note: The expression **were born** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [were descendants of Rapha in Gath]

Here, **hand** represents the power and capability of David and his servants to defeat these enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they fell by the power of David and by the power of his servants]
See how you translated the term **fell** in 5:10. Alternate translation: [And they died at the hands of David and his servants] or [And it was David and his servants who killed them]

The author is crediting David in part with these victories because he commanded the Israelite soldiers who won them. But he is then crediting the specific **servants** or soldiers who defeated these giant opponents. If the connection between the first part of this phrase and the second part is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word or phrase to show how the parts relate to one another. Alternate translation: [by the hand of David and, specifically, by the hands of his servants]
